A Fern Waiting for Rain

Resurrection ferns often grow on tree branches in humid forests. During a long dry period, their green fronds curl inward and turn brown. The change can make a living fern resemble a dead one.

Growing along the bark, dry air removes water from the fern's fronds.[1] As cells lose water, the fronds fold so that less surface area faces sunlight and moving air. The cells retain membranes and other structures needed to resume ordinary activity when water returns.[2]

After rain, the plant absorbs moisture and unfolds in a rapid amount of time.[3] A series of protective changes allow[4] its cells to tolerate the shift from a hydrated state to a dry one and back again. The fern can then resume photosynthesis.

The common name does not mean that the plant actually dies and returns to life. Severe or prolonged conditions can still damage it. The fern's remarkable ability is more precise: it can suspend much of its visible activity during drought while preserving the cellular organization needed to recover when water becomes available.[5]
